claims.text: Al0.5CoCrFeNi is a lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The initial as-cast Al0.5CoCrFeNi alloy is homogeneous and single-phase.
Aging Al0.5CoCrFeNi at 500–600 °C induces nanoscale coherent precipitates.
The aging-induced precipitates are uniformly dispersed through the alloy matrix.
Precipitate formation increases the yield strength of the aged Al0.5CoCrFeNi alloy.
The precipitates restrict diffusion pathways for oxygen.
The precipitates restrict diffusion pathways for corrosive species.
Aging-induced precipitates improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast baseline.
Aging-induced precipitates improve corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast baseline.
The strengthening, corrosion, and oxidation benefits persist only while the precipitates remain finely dispersed and stable.
Temperatures above approximately 700 °C or excessively long aging cause precipitate coarsening or dissolution in Al0.5CoCrFeNi.
Precipitate coarsening or dissolution causes the strength, corrosion, and oxidation benefits to diminish to performance similar to or worse than the untreated baseline.
Homogeneously distributed precipitates improve yield strength in related lightweight refractory high-entropy alloys.
Heat treatment can improve corrosion resistance in a Cantor alloy through grain growth and formation of a Cr2O3-rich passive layer.
The exact critical aging temperature and duration for precipitate stability in Al0.5CoCrFeNi are not established.
High-temperature exposure at approximately 900 °C can be used to evaluate the proposed oxidation benefit of the aged alloy.
Observation of performance improvements without stable nanoprecipitates would falsify the proposed precipitate-mediated mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as as-cast, while the baseline is described as both as-cast and homogenized. Homogenization is a post-casting heat treatment, so these are not necessarily the same untreated state.

Oxidation and corrosion benefits are to be evaluated at approximately 900 °C, but the hypothesis states that temperatures above approximately 700 °C cause precipitate instability and loss of those benefits. The predicted direction at 900 °C is therefore internally ambiguous unless exposure time or precipitate stability is further qualified.
